Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
A specific texture associated with the event

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette: Rosa was twenty-two when the mortar round struck the perimeter of the forward camp. She remembered the initial boom as a concussive wave that swallowed the air, followed by the sharp, rolling crashes of secondary explosions. Amid the dust, she had pulled a young medic away from the collapsed sandbags, her hands pressed against the coarse, woven texture of his torn uniform as the color drained from his face. In the chaos, another comrade bled out nearby, leaving behind a pile of unopened letters that spoke of families and lost time. When Rosa finally returned home, the past did not stay buried. Whenever she heard a loud bang or found herself listening to someone describe losing a parent, her breath would catch and her pulse would hammer against her ribs, as if her body had never stopped bracing for the next strike. The coarse fabric of that torn uniform, the rolling crashes, and casual conversations about funerals pulled her directly into the fragmented recollections of the attack, which refused to settle into a linear timeline. She found herself unable to piece together whether she had moved the medic before or after the secondary blasts, and when she tried to recount the incident to anyone, the details dissolved into a blur that she could not finish explaining. The fragments felt so extreme and detached from reality that she began to doubt whether the event had actually happened to her or belonged to a nightmare. Yet the unresolved, shifting recollections constantly primed her nervous system, making her shoulders tense and her breath shallow the moment a door slammed or a conversation turned toward loss. Her constant scanning and physical reactivity kept her nervous system in a state of constant alert, which made her notice loud bangs and loss themes even more readily. Over the years, this relentless scanning and the constant physical jolts of alertness rewired her understanding of the world, convincing her that safety was an illusion and that nothing she did anymore could hold real meaning. These sudden intrusions of the past, in turn, solidified her conviction that the world remained a dangerous place and that her life had lost its meaning. As a bank teller, the daily routine became a minefield of these reinforced fears. The heavy clunk of the coin drop mechanism at the end of the day would send her reflexively ducking behind the counter, her hands shaking as she checked the security logs. Customers’ neutral expressions were no longer just polite pauses; they were read as concealed hostility, which is why she began avoiding the drive-through lane and stopped making eye contact during teller transactions. The gradual withdrawal from her social circle and the loss of her previous career left her with a profound sense of emptiness. Now at fifty-five, Rosa finally walked into a clinic after her daughter gently confronted her about the way she slept with a baseball bat beside the bed and jumped at the sound of a car backfiring. What frightened her most was not the memories themselves, but the certainty that her body and mind were permanently wired for survival in a combat zone that no longer existed. She hoped to find a way to quiet the constant alarm, to trust that a loud noise was just a noise, and to look at the world without the exhausting weight of perpetual threat.
